bal.17.so17: I bow to Hanumān, son of the Wind, a fire to the forest of the wicked, full of wisdom.
In the house of his heart Śrī Rāma dwells, holding his bow and arrows.
aranya.0.shloka1: The root of the tree of dharma, the full moon that gladdens the ocean of discernment,
the sun to the lotus of dispassion, who surely drives off the dense darkness of sin and takes away affliction,
the wind born of the sky in scattering the massed clouds of delusion, Śaṅkara,
sprung from Brahmā's line, remover of stain, dear to King Śrī Rāma: to him I bow.
aranya.0.shloka2: Whose body, full of dense bliss, has the beauty of a rain cloud, clad in yellow and lovely,
with bow and arrow in his hand and a fine quiver gleaming at his waist,
with long lotus eyes, graced by the matted locks he wears,
walking the road with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa: him, the delightful Rāma, I worship.
aranya.0.sou1: Umā, Śrī Rāma's virtues are deep; learned men and sages gain dispassion from them.
Those who are deluded, turned away from Śrī Hari and without love for dharma, are led by them into delusion.
aranya.1.cau1: I have sung, as far as my understanding allows, the love of the townspeople and of Bharata, matchless and lovely.
Now hear the Lord's most holy deeds, done in the forest, which delight gods, men and sages.
aranya.1.cau2: Once Śrī Rāma gathered lovely flowers and made ornaments with his own hands.
The Lord put them on Sītā with loving care and sat on a beautiful slab of crystal.
aranya.1.cau3: Indra's son, the wretch, disguised himself as a crow and wanted to see how strong Śrī Rāma was,
as though an ant, utterly slow of mind, wanted to reach the bottom of the ocean.
aranya.1.cau4: Pecking Sītā's foot with his beak, the foolish, dull-witted creature fled, a crow only for a purpose.
The blood flowed; Śrī Rāma knew of it and set a reed to his bow as an arrow.
aranya.1.do1: Śrī Rāma is supremely compassionate, ever loving towards the lowly.
With him that fool, a house of faults, came and played a trick.
aranya.2.cau1: Driven by a mantra, the Brahmā arrow sped after him; the crow took fright and fled.
Taking his own form he went to his father, but his father would not keep one turned against Śrī Rāma.
aranya.2.cau2: He lost hope, and terror arose in his mind, as it did in the sage Durvāsā for fear of the discus.
Brahmā's realm, Śiva's city, every world he wandered, weary and frantic with fear and grief.
aranya.2.cau3: No one even asked him to sit. Who can shelter one who is hostile to Śrī Rāma?
Listen, Garuḍa: to such a one his mother becomes death, his father becomes like Yama, and nectar turns to poison.
aranya.2.cau4: A friend behaves to him like a hundred enemies, and the river of the gods becomes for him the Vaitaraṇī, the river of hell.
Listen, brother: to one who turns from Śrī Rāma the whole world grows hotter than fire.
aranya.2.cau5: Nārada saw Jayanta in distress, and pity touched him, for the hearts of saints are tender.
He sent him at once to Śrī Rāma, and Jayanta cried out: Friend of those who bow before you, save me.
aranya.2.cau6: Anxious and afraid, he went and clasped his feet: Save me, save me, compassionate Lord of the Raghus.
Your strength is beyond compare, and so is your sovereignty; I, slow of mind, could not grasp it.
aranya.2.cau7: I have reaped the fruit of my own deeds. Now protect me, Lord; I have come looking to you for refuge.
Hearing his most piteous words, Pārvatī, the compassionate Lord left him with one eye and let him go.
aranya.2.so2: Under delusion he had shown enmity, and though it was right that he be slain,
the Lord spared him out of tenderness. Who is as compassionate as Śrī Rāma?
aranya.3.cau1: Living at Citrakūṭa, Śrī Rāma did many deeds that are like nectar to the ear.
Then Śrī Rāma reflected: Everyone knows me now; crowds will gather here.
aranya.3.cau2: With leave taken of every sage, the two brothers went on their way, Sītā with them.
The Lord arrived at Atri's hermitage; hearing of it, the great sage rejoiced.
aranya.3.cau3: Atri, the hair on his body standing on end, rose and ran; when Śrī Rāma saw this he came on in haste.
The brothers were still lying prostrate when the sage pressed them to his heart, and he bathed them both in loving tears.
aranya.3.cau4: Seeing Śrī Rāma's beauty brought coolness to the sage's eyes; then he led them respectfully to his own hermitage.
After worship and gracious words he offered roots and fruit, which pleased the Lord.
aranya.3.so3: The Lord is seated; gazing at his beauty till his eyes are full,
the great sage, supremely wise, joins his palms and sings his praise:
aranya.4.cha1: I salute you, loving to your devotees, compassionate, gentle of nature.
I worship your lotus feet, which give your own abode to those who desire nothing.
aranya.4.cha2: Dark and surpassingly beautiful, you are Mount Mandara to churn the ocean of worldly existence.
Your eyes are like full-blown lotuses; you set us free from pride and the other faults.
aranya.4.cha3: Long of arm and mighty in valour, O Lord, your splendour is beyond measure.
You bear quiver, bow and arrows; you are the lord of the three worlds.
aranya.4.cha4: You are the jewel of the solar race and the breaker of Śiva's bow;
you delight the great sages and the saints and shatter the throngs of the gods' foes.
aranya.4.cha5: Śiva, the foe of Kāmadeva, bows to you; Brahmā and the other gods serve you;
your form is pure awareness, and you take away every fault.
aranya.4.cha6: I salute you, lord of Indirā (Lakṣmī), source of happiness, goal of the good.
I worship you with your Śakti (Sītā) and your younger brother, you who are the dear younger brother (Upendra) of Indra, Śacī's lord.
aranya.4.cha7: Those who, free of envy, worship at the soles of your feet
do not fall into the ocean of worldly existence, crowded with waves of doubt.
aranya.4.cha8: Those who dwell ever in solitude and joyfully worship you for liberation
draw back the senses and the rest, and reach their own true state.
aranya.4.cha9: Him, the one and wondrous Lord, desireless, the Master, all-pervading,
the teacher of the world, eternal, the Fourth (turīya, beyond waking, dream and sleep), the one alone,
aranya.4.cha10: him I worship, who loves true feeling and is very hard to reach for those of false practice;
a wish-fulfilling tree to his own devotees, impartial, easy to serve day after day.
aranya.4.cha11: King of peerless beauty, husband of the earth-born Sītā, I bow to you.
Look kindly on me; I salute you; give me devotion to your lotus feet.
aranya.4.cha12: Those who recite this hymn with reverence
go to your abode, filled with devotion to you; of this there is no doubt.
aranya.4.do4: Having made his prayer, the sage bowed his head, then joined his palms and said:
My Lord, may my mind never leave your lotus feet.
aranya.5.cau1: Clasping Anasūyā's feet, Sītā, gentle and humble, then greeted her.
Joy grew in the heart of the sage's wife; she blessed her and seated her close by.
aranya.5.cau2: She dressed her in heavenly clothes and ornaments that stay ever new, spotless and lovely.
The sage's wife spoke in sweet, tender words and, using Sītā as her pretext, described something of a woman's dharma:
aranya.5.cau3: Mother, father and brother are all your well-wishers, but listen, princess: what any of them gives has limits.
A husband, Vaidehī, is a giver beyond all measure, and a woman who does not serve him is base.
aranya.5.cau4: Patience, dharma, a friend and a wife: these four are tested in times of trouble.
A husband may be old, sickly, dull, poor, blind, deaf, quick to anger or utterly wretched;
aranya.5.cau5: yet a wife who slights even such a husband suffers many torments in Yama's city.
She has one dharma, one vow, one rule: to love her husband's feet in body, word and mind.
aranya.5.cau6: The Vedas, the Purāṇas and all the saints say that a faithful wife is of four kinds in this world.
In the mind of the highest kind it is settled that no other man exists in the world, even in a dream.
aranya.5.cau7: The middling one looks on another man as she would on her own brother, father or son.
She who holds back thinking of dharma and mindful of her family, the Veda calls the lower kind.
aranya.5.cau8: And she who stays faithful only for lack of opportunity or out of fear, count her as the lowest kind of woman in the world.
She who deceives her husband and loves another man falls into the Raurava hell for a hundred kalpas (ages).
aranya.5.cau9: For a moment's pleasure she does not see the sorrow of a hundred crore births: who is as wicked as she?
A woman who gives up deceit and holds to the dharma of a faithful wife reaches the supreme state without toil.
aranya.5.cau10: She who goes against her husband, wherever she is born, is widowed as she reaches youth.
aranya.5.so5क: Though a woman is impure by nature, by serving her husband she attains a blessed state.
The four Vedas sing the fame of Tulasī, who is dear to Śrī Hari even today.
aranya.5.so5ख: Listen, Sītā: by remembering your name women keep faith with their husbands.
Śrī Rāma is as dear to you as life; I have told this for the good of the world.
aranya.6.cau1: Hearing this, Sītā was filled with joy and bowed her head with reverence at Anasūyā's feet.
Then Śrī Rāma, the treasury of mercy, said to the sage: If you permit, I shall now go to another forest.
aranya.6.cau2: Keep showing me your grace always, and knowing me for your servant, never withdraw your love.
At these words of the Lord, the mainstay of dharma, the wise sage answered with love:
aranya.6.cau3: Whose grace Brahmā, Śiva, Sanaka and his brothers and all who speak of the highest truth seek:
you are that very one, Rāma, dear to the desireless, friend of the lowly, who now speak such gentle words.
aranya.6.cau4: Now I see how clever Śrī (Lakṣmī) was, who passed over all the gods and gave herself to you.
How should he whom none can equal or surpass not have such goodness of nature?
aranya.6.cau5: How can I tell you, my master, to go now? Say it yourself, my Lord, for you know every heart.
With these words the steadfast sage gazed at the Lord, tears flowing from his eyes and his body thrilling.
aranya.6.cha1: The sage is thrilled all over and filled to the brim with love; he has fixed his eyes on the lotus of the Lord's face.
He thinks: What japa and austerity did I perform, that I have seen the Lord who is beyond mind, knowledge, the guṇas and the senses?
By japa, yoga and the many works of dharma a person comes to devotion beyond compare.
The servant Tulasīdāsa sings the holy deeds of Śrī Rāma night and day.
aranya.6.do6क: Śrī Rāma's fair fame wipes away the impurity of the Kali age, masters the mind and is the root of happiness.
Those who hear it with reverence have Śrī Rāma ever on their side.
aranya.6.so6ख: This hard age is a storehouse of impurity; in it there is no dharma, no knowledge, no yoga, no japa.
Those who give up all reliance on anything else and worship Śrī Rāma are wise.
aranya.7.cau1: Śrī Rāma, Lord of gods, men and sages, laid his head at the sage's lotus feet and set off into the forest.
Śrī Rāma walks in front and his younger brother behind him, both splendid in the fine garb of hermits.
aranya.7.cau2: Between the two, how does Sītā look? Like māyā (the Lord's power of illusion) between Brahman and the individual soul.
Rivers, forests, mountains and rugged passes know their Lord and open a good way for him.
aranya.7.cau3: Wherever the divine Śrī Rāma goes, clouds spread shade across the sky.
As they went along the way, the demon Virādha met them; the moment he came near, Śrī Rāma struck him down.
aranya.7.cau4: At once he gained a beautiful form; seeing him in sorrow, the Lord sent him to his own abode.
Then, with his handsome younger brother and Sītā, he came to where the sage Śarabhaṅga lived.
aranya.7.do7: The great sage's eyes, like bees, gaze on Śrī Rāma's lotus face
and reverently drink in its nectar; most blessed is Śarabhaṅga's birth.
aranya.8.cau1: The sage said: Listen, compassionate hero of the Raghus, royal swan of the Mānasa lake of Śiva's mind.
I was on my way to Brahmā's realm when I heard that Śrī Rāma would come to the forest.
aranya.8.cau2: Day and night I kept watching the road; now, seeing my Lord, my heart is at peace.
My Lord, I am bare of every spiritual practice; knowing me for a lowly servant, you have shown me grace.
aranya.8.cau3: Yet this is no favour to me, my Lord; you have kept your own vow, you who steal your devotees' hearts.
Until I give up this body and come to you, stay here for the good of this humble one.
aranya.8.cau4: Yoga, sacrifice, japa, austerity and vows, all that he had practised, he offered up to the Lord, and from him took the boon of devotion.
Having thus built a pyre, the sage Śarabhaṅga sat on it, his heart free of every attachment.
aranya.8.do8: Lord, with Sītā and your younger brother, dark of body as a blue rain cloud,
Śrī Rāma in form with attributes, dwell in my heart for ever.
aranya.9.cau1: Saying this, he burnt his body in the fire of yoga and by Śrī Rāma's grace went to Vaikuṇṭha.
He did not merge into Śrī Hari, because he had already taken the boon of devotion that keeps the servant distinct from the Lord.
aranya.9.cau2: Seeing the state the great sage had reached, the assembled seers were especially glad at heart.
The whole company of sages sings his praise: Glory to the Lord who cares for those who bow to him, the root of compassion!
aranya.9.cau3: Then Śrī Rāma went on further into the forest, and many bands of great sages went along with him.
Seeing heaps of bones, Śrī Rāma was moved to great pity and asked the sages about them.
aranya.9.cau4: The sages said: Why do you ask, Lord, when you already know? You see all and dwell within every heart.
Hordes of demons have eaten all these sages. Hearing this, Śrī Rāma's eyes filled with tears.
aranya.9.do9: Raising his arm, Śrī Rāma vowed: I will rid the earth of demons.
and he visited the hermitage of every sage in turn, bringing each of them joy.
aranya.10.cau1: The sage Agastya had a wise disciple named Sutīkṣṇa, who loved the Lord.
In thought, deed and word he served Śrī Rāma's feet, and not even in a dream did he rely on any other god.
aranya.10.cau2: As soon as he heard of the Lord's coming, he ran off in eagerness, building hopes as he went.
O Creator, will Śrī Rāma, friend of the lowly, show mercy to a wretch like me?
aranya.10.cau3: Will Śrī Rāma, my master, with his younger brother, meet me as one of his own servants?
I have no firm confidence in my heart; there is no devotion, dispassion or knowledge in my mind.
aranya.10.cau4: I have had no company of the good, no yoga, japa or sacrifice, no firm love for the lotus feet.
But the treasury of compassion has one way: dear to him is the one who has no other refuge.
aranya.10.cau5: Today my eyes will be fulfilled, seeing the lotus face of him who frees from worldly existence.
The wise sage is wholly immersed in love; his state, Pārvatī, is beyond words.
aranya.10.cau6: He cannot tell the quarters or the points between them, nor the path; who he is and where he is going he does not know.
Now he turns back, then goes on again; now he sings the Lord's virtues and dances.
aranya.10.cau7: The sage has found unbroken, loving devotion; the Lord watches him, hidden behind a tree.
Seeing his boundless love, Śrī Rāma, who removes the fears of worldly existence, appeared in his heart.
aranya.10.cau8: The sage sat motionless in the middle of the path, his body bristling with thrill like a jackfruit.
Then Śrī Rāma came up close; seeing his devotee in that state, he was pleased at heart.
aranya.10.cau9: In many ways Śrī Rāma tried to wake the sage, but he did not stir, enjoying the bliss that meditation brought.
Then Śrī Rāma concealed his royal form, and within the sage's heart showed himself with four arms.
aranya.10.cau10: The sage then started up in distress, like a great serpent that has lost its jewel.
Before him he saw Śrī Rāma, dark of body, the home of joy, with Sītā and his younger brother.
aranya.10.cau11: Like a staff the fortunate sage fell at his feet, lost in love.
With his long arms the Lord lifted him up and held him to his breast with the deepest love.
aranya.10.cau12: As he embraces the sage, the compassionate Lord looks like a tamāla tree embracing a tree of gold.
The sage stands gazing at Śrī Rāma's face, as still as a figure drawn in a picture.
aranya.10.do10: Then the sage steadied his heart and clasped the Lord's feet again and again.
He brought the Lord to his hermitage and worshipped him in many ways.
aranya.11.cau1: The sage said: Lord, hear my prayer. How am I to praise you?
Your greatness is boundless, my understanding small, like a firefly's glow before the sun.
aranya.11.cau2: Dark of body like a garland of blue lotuses, wearing a crown of matted hair and a hermit's bark clothing,
bow and arrows in hand, quiver at the waist: to Śrī Rāma I bow without ceasing.
aranya.11.cau3: A fire to burn the dense forest of delusion, a sun to the lotus groves of the saints,
a lion to the herds of demon elephants, a hawk to the bird of worldly existence: may he ever protect us.
aranya.11.cau4: With eyes like red lotuses and fair attire, a moon to the cakora birds of Sītā's eyes,
a young swan in the Mānasa lake of Śiva's heart: to Rāma, broad of chest and long of arm, I bow.
aranya.11.cau5: A Garuḍa to swallow the serpent of doubt, the soother of grief born of harsh argument,
breaker of worldly existence, delight of the hosts of gods, a mass of grace: may he ever protect us.
aranya.11.cau6: Without attributes and with them, unequal and equal, beyond knowledge, speech and the senses, matchless,
pure, entire, faultless and boundless: to Rāma, remover of the earth's burden, I bow.
aranya.11.cau7: A garden of wish-granting trees for his devotees, who drives off anger, greed, pride and desire,
supremely wise, a bridge over the ocean of worldly existence: may the banner of the Sun's race ever protect us.
aranya.11.cau8: Abode of matchless strength and might of arm, whose name shatters the vast stain of the Kali age,
armour of dharma, a store of joy-giving virtues: may my Rāma ever bring me blessing.
aranya.11.cau9: Though he is pure, all-pervading and imperishable, ever dwelling in every heart,
yet may Śrī Rāma, slayer of Khara, who roams the forest, dwell in my mind with his younger brother and Sītā.
aranya.11.cau10: Let those who know, my Lord, know you as with and without attributes, the inner ruler of the heart;
but may Rāma, the lotus-eyed Lord of Kosala, make my heart his home.
aranya.11.cau11: May this pride never leave me, even by oversight: I am the servant, and Śrī Rāma is my master.
The sage's words delighted Śrī Rāma; joyfully he embraced the great sage once more.
aranya.11.cau12: Śrī Rāma said: Know that I am supremely pleased, sage; whatever boon you ask, I will give you.
The sage said: I have never asked for a boon; I cannot tell what is false and what is true.
aranya.11.cau13: Lord of the Raghus, giver of joy to your servants, give me whatever seems good to you.
Śrī Rāma said: May you have unbroken devotion, dispassion and realised knowledge, and become a treasury of every virtue and of wisdom.
aranya.11.cau14: The sage said: The boon my Lord gave, I have received; now give me what I long for.
aranya.11.do11: Lord Rāma, bearing bow and arrows, with your younger brother and Sītā,
dwell for ever in the sky of my heart like the moon, free of desire.
aranya.12.cau1: Saying so be it, Śrī Rāma, abode of Lakṣmī, joyfully set out for the pot-born sage Agastya.
Sutīkṣṇa said: It has been many days since I had sight of my guru and settled in this hermitage.
aranya.12.cau2: Now I will go with my Lord to my guru; in this, my Lord, I put you under no obligation.
Seeing the sage's cleverness, the treasury of mercy took him along, and both brothers laughed.
aranya.12.cau3: Speaking along the way of devotion to himself, beyond compare, Śrī Rāma, king of the gods, reached the sage's hermitage.
Sutīkṣṇa went at once to his guru, prostrated himself, and spoke thus:
aranya.12.cau4: My lord, the son of the king of Kosala, the support of the world, has come to meet you:
It is Śrī Rāma, the very one whose name you chant day and night, my master, and with him are his younger brother and Sītā.
aranya.12.cau5: Hearing this, Agastya sprang up and hurried out; tears welled in his eyes as he beheld Śrī Hari.
Both brothers threw themselves at the sage's lotus feet, and the seer, full of love, held them to his heart.
aranya.12.cau6: The wise sage asked after their welfare with respect, then brought them and seated them on fine seats.
Then, after worshipping the Lord in many ways, he said: There is no one as fortunate as I.
aranya.12.cau7: All the other companies of sages who were there rejoiced to see him, the root of joy.
aranya.12.do12: In the midst of the gathered sages the Lord sits facing every one of them.
They gaze at him as a flock of cakora birds gazes at the autumn moon.
aranya.13.cau1: Then Śrī Rāma said to the sage: My lord, nothing is hidden from you.
You know the reason for which I have come; that is why, revered sir, I have not spelt it out.
aranya.13.cau2: Now, my lord, give me the counsel by which I may slay the enemies of the sages.
Hearing the Lord's words the sage smiled and said: My Lord, what did you take me to be, that you asked me this?
aranya.13.cau3: O destroyer of sin, it is only by the power of worshipping you that I know a little of your glory.
Your māyā is a vast cluster-fig tree, and its fruits are the many hosts of universes.
aranya.13.cau4: Living beings, moving and unmoving, dwell within those fruits like tiny creatures and know of nothing else.
The eater of those fruits is harsh and dreadful Time, and even that Time is ever afraid of you.
aranya.13.cau5: And you, the master of all the guardians of the worlds, have questioned me as a man would.
This boon I ask, O abode of grace: dwell in my heart with Sītā and your younger brother.
aranya.13.cau6: Grant me unceasing devotion, dispassion, the company of the good, and unbroken love for your lotus feet.
Although you are Brahman, indivisible and endless, known only through experience and worshipped by the saints,
aranya.13.cau7: and though I know that form of yours and describe it, again and again it is Brahman with attributes that I love.
You always give honour to your servants; that is why, O Lord of the Raghus, you have asked me.
aranya.13.cau8: My Lord, there is a most charming place; its name is holy Pañcavaṭī.
Make the Daṇḍaka forest pure, my Lord, and lift the great sage's fierce curse.
aranya.13.cau9: Live there, O king of Raghu's race, and be kind to all the sages.
With the sage's leave Śrī Rāma went on his way and was soon near Pañcavaṭī.
aranya.13.do13: There he met Jaṭāyu, king of the vultures, and their love grew in many ways.
Near the Godāvarī the Lord thatched a hut of leaves and made his home there.
aranya.14.cau1: Ever since Śrī Rāma made his home there, the sages were happy and their fear was gone.
Hills, forests, rivers and lakes were filled with beauty, and grew lovelier with every passing day.
aranya.14.cau2: Flocks of birds and herds of deer lived in joy, and the bees, humming sweetly, made a lovely sight.
That forest, where Śrī Rāma dwelt in visible form, not even Śeṣa, king of serpents, could describe.
aranya.14.cau3: One day the Lord sat at ease, and Lakṣmaṇa spoke to him in words free of all deceit:
Master of gods, men and sages and of all that moves and does not move, I ask you as I would ask my own lord.
aranya.14.cau4: Explain to me, my Lord, that by which I may leave everything and serve the dust of your feet.
Tell me of knowledge, dispassion and māyā, and tell me of the devotion for whose sake you show mercy.
aranya.14.do14: My Lord, explain to me as well the whole difference between God and the individual soul.
Through that, may love for your feet arise, and grief, delusion and error depart.
aranya.15.cau1: Śrī Rāma said: I will explain it all in a few words, dear brother; listen with your understanding, mind and heart intent.
The sense of I and mine, of you and yours, is māyā, which holds all the hosts of beings in its sway.
aranya.15.cau2: The senses, their objects, and all that the mind can reach, brother: know all of it to be māyā.
Hear also its divisions; there are two, the one knowledge (vidyā), the other ignorance (avidyā).
aranya.15.cau3: One, ignorance, is wicked and full of sorrow beyond measure; in its power the soul has fallen into the well of worldly existence.
The other, knowledge, which holds the guṇas (the qualities of nature) under its sway, creates the world; it acts as the Lord impels it, with no strength of its own.
aranya.15.cau4: Knowledge is that in which not a trace of pride remains, and which sees Brahman equally in all.
Dear brother, that one should be called supremely dispassionate who has cast off the siddhis (powers) and the three guṇas as if they were straw.
aranya.15.do15: One who does not know māyā, God or his own self should be called the soul (jīva).
He who grants bondage and liberation, who is beyond all and sets māyā in motion, is the Lord, the auspicious one.
aranya.16.cau1: From dharma comes dispassion, from yoga knowledge, and knowledge grants liberation: so the Vedas declare.
But that by which I quickly melt, brother, is devotion to me, which gives joy to my devotees.
aranya.16.cau2: It is free and needs nothing else to lean on; knowledge and realised knowledge are under its control.
Dear brother, devotion has no equal and is the source of all happiness; it comes to one when the saints are pleased.
aranya.16.cau3: Now I shall set out in full what leads to devotion: it is an easy road, and by it living beings attain me.
First comes deep love for the feet of the brāhmaṇas, and each being devoted to his own duties in the way the Vedas teach.
aranya.16.cau4: Its fruit, in turn, is dispassion towards the objects of sense; then love springs up for my dharma.
The nine forms of devotion, hearing and the rest, grow firm, and the mind holds deep love for my divine play (līlā).
aranya.16.cau5: There should be deep love for the saints' lotus feet, and a firm rule of worship in mind, deed and word.
One should know me as guru, father, mother, brother, lord and god, all in one, and be steadfast in service.
aranya.16.cau6: As he sings my virtues, his body thrills, his voice is choked and tears flow from his eyes.
Dear brother, one in whom there is no desire and the like, no pride and no hypocrisy: I am ever under his sway.
aranya.16.do16: Those whose refuge I am in word, deed and mind, and who worship without desire,
in the lotus of their hearts I ever take my rest.
aranya.17.cau1: Hearing of the path of devotion, Lakṣmaṇa felt great joy and bowed his head at the Lord's feet.
In this way some days went by in talk of dispassion, knowledge, virtues and right conduct.
aranya.17.cau2: Śūrpaṇakhā, Rāvaṇa's sister, was wicked of heart and as cruel as a female serpent.
Once she went to Pañcavaṭī, and at the sight of the two princes she was overcome.
aranya.17.cau3: Garuḍa, a woman who sees a charming man, be he brother, father or son, is stirred.
She cannot hold back her mind, as the sunstone melts at the sight of the sun.
aranya.17.cau4: Taking on a lovely form, she went to the Lord and, smiling broadly, said:
No man is your equal, and no woman mine; the Creator has made this match after careful thought.
aranya.17.cau5: I have searched the three worlds and found no man anywhere to match me.
That is why I have stayed unmarried until now; seeing you, my heart is somewhat content.
aranya.17.cau6: Glancing at Sītā, the Lord said: My younger brother is unmarried.
She went to Lakṣmaṇa; knowing her to be the enemy's sister, he looked at the Lord and spoke gently:
aranya.17.cau7: Listen, fair one: I am his servant. I am not my own master; there would be no comfort for you with me.
My Lord is able to do anything; he is the king of Kosalapura, and whatever he does becomes him.
aranya.17.cau8: A servant who wants comfort, a beggar honour, one given to vice wealth, a profligate a blessed end,
a greedy man fame, a proud man the four ends of life: these creatures look for milk by milking the sky.
aranya.17.cau9: She turned back and came once more to Śrī Rāma; the Lord sent her again to Lakṣmaṇa.
Lakṣmaṇa said: He will wed you who has cut every tie with shame and cast it off.
aranya.17.cau10: Then, stung and angry, she went to Śrī Rāma and revealed her terrible form.
When he saw Sītā frightened, Śrī Rāma signalled to his brother and told him what to do.
aranya.17.do17: With great swiftness Lakṣmaṇa left her without nose and ears.
It was as though he had sent Rāvaṇa a challenge by her hand.
aranya.18.cau1: Robbed of nose and ears she was hideous to see, as if a mountain were pouring out streams of red ochre.
Weeping, she went to Khara and Dūṣaṇa and cried: Shame, shame on your manhood and your strength, brother!
aranya.18.cau2: When he asked, she told him everything plainly; hearing it, the demons made ready an army.
Hosts upon hosts of demons rushed out, like flocks of winged mountains of lampblack.
aranya.18.cau3: On mounts of many kinds, in many shapes, terrible and past counting, they carried weapons of every sort.
They put Śūrpaṇakhā at their head, ill-omened to look at, without ears or nose.
aranya.18.cau4: Countless fearful ill omens appeared, but all of them, in the grip of death, paid them no heed.
They roared, they threatened, they leapt into the sky; the warriors rejoiced greatly at the sight of the army.
aranya.18.cau5: Someone shouted: Take both brothers alive! Seize them, put them to death, and snatch the woman away.
The whole sky was filled with dust. Śrī Rāma called his younger brother and said:
aranya.18.cau6: Take Sītā and go to a mountain cave; a fearsome army of demons has come.
Stay on your guard. Hearing the Lord's words, Lakṣmaṇa went with Sītā, bow and arrows in hand.
aranya.18.cau7: Seeing the enemy host advancing, Śrī Rāma smiled and strung his mighty bow.
aranya.18.cha1: Having strung the mighty bow, as he binds his matted locks into a knot upon his head, how splendid he looks:
like a pair of serpents fighting with countless lightnings on a mountain of emerald.
Girding the quiver at his waist, taking the bow in his long arms and setting the arrows right,
the Lord gazes as a lion gazes when it sees a herd of mighty elephants.
aranya.18.so18: The warriors came charging in close array, crying out to seize him, seize him.
They closed round him as demons close round the young sun when they see it alone.
aranya.19.cau1: Seeing the Lord, they could not loose their arrows; the demon host stood spellbound.
Khara and Dūṣaṇa called their minister and said: This is some prince, a jewel among men.
aranya.19.cau2: Of nāgas, asuras, gods, men and sages, how many have we seen, conquered and slain!
Listen, brothers all: in our whole lives we have never seen such beauty.
aranya.19.cau3: Though he has disfigured our sister, so peerless a man does not deserve to be slain.
Hand over at once the woman you have hidden, and go home alive, the two of you.
aranya.19.cau4: Tell him what I have said, and when you have heard his reply, come back quickly.
The messengers went and told Śrī Rāma; on hearing it, Śrī Rāma smiled and said:
aranya.19.cau5: We are kṣatriyas who hunt in the forest, and it is beasts like you, wicked ones, that we roam in search of.
We do not fear a mighty foe when we see one; we would fight even Death, for once.
aranya.19.cau6: Men though we are, we destroy the race of demons; boys though we are, we guard the sages and torment the wicked.
If you lack the strength, turn back home; I strike down no one who turns away from battle.
aranya.19.cau7: Once in battle, to use guile and cunning, or to show mercy to an enemy, is the worst cowardice.
The messengers went and quickly told it all, and hearing it, Khara and Dūṣaṇa burned with rage at heart.
aranya.19.cha1: Their hearts ablaze, they cried: Seize him. The fearsome demon warriors charged.
They bore arrows, bows, javelins, spears, tridents, swords, iron clubs and axes.
First the Lord twanged his bow, with a harsh, terrible and fearful sound.
The demons were deafened and dismayed; at that moment they had no sense left.
aranya.19.do19क: Knowing the foe to be strong, they rushed on, now on their guard.
They began to rain missiles and weapons of many kinds upon Śrī Rāma.
aranya.19.do19ख: Śrī Rāma cut their weapons into pieces as small as sesame seeds.
Then, drawing his bow to his ear, he loosed his own arrows.
aranya.20.cha1: Then the terrible arrows flew, like a host of hissing serpents.
Śrī Rāma grew wrathful in the battle, and his arrows, keen beyond measure, sped on.
aranya.20.cau2: Seeing those razor-sharp arrows, the demon warriors turned and fled.
The three brothers grew angry and said: Whoever runs away from the battle,
aranya.20.cau3: him we shall slay with our own hands. At this they turned back, resolved in their hearts to die.
Now they stood face to face and struck with weapons of many kinds.
aranya.20.cau4: Knowing the foe to be in a towering rage, the Lord set an arrow to his bow.
He loosed a great many iron shafts, and the dreadful fiends began to be cut down.
aranya.20.cau5: Chests, heads, arms, hands and feet began to fall on the ground on every side.
As the arrows struck, the demons shrieked, and their trunks came down like mountains.
aranya.20.cau6: Warriors are cut down, their bodies in a hundred pieces, and still they rise again through their tricks.
Arms and heads in great numbers fly through the air, and headless trunks run about.
aranya.20.cau7: Birds, the kaṅka and the crow, and jackals gnash their teeth, harsh and dreadful.
aranya.20.cha1_2: Jackals gnash their teeth; ghosts, spirits and fiends go about filling their skull-bowls.
Heroic vetālas beat time on skulls, and the yoginīs dance.
Śrī Rāma's fierce arrows sever the warriors' chests, arms and heads.
Their trunks drop here and there, then rise and fight on, raising a fearful cry: Seize him, seize him.
aranya.20.cha2: Vultures fly off clutching entrails, and fiends run holding the other end in their hands,
as though many children who dwell in the city of battle were flying kites.
Warriors in great numbers lie slain or dashed down, their chests torn open, groaning.
Seeing their army in distress, Triśirā and the other champions, with Khara and Dūṣaṇa, turned to fight.
aranya.20.cha3: Arrows, spears, javelins, axes, tridents and swords, all at a single moment,
countless demons hurl in their fury at Śrī Rāma.
Within a moment the Lord had stopped the foe's arrows; then he called out his challenge and shot his own.
Into the chest of every demon chief he drove ten arrows apiece.
aranya.20.cha4: No sooner do the warriors fall to earth than they rise and close again; they do not die, and they weave thick illusions.
The gods are afraid to see fourteen thousand fiends against the Lord of Avadh alone.
Seeing the gods and sages in fear, the Lord, master of māyā, worked a great marvel.
The foes began to see one another as Rāma, and the enemy host fought among itself and perished.
aranya.20.do20क: Crying Rāma, Rāma, they leave their bodies and reach the state of liberation.
By this device Śrī Rāma, the treasury of mercy, slew the enemy in an instant.
aranya.20.do20ख: The gods in their joy rain down flowers, and drums sound in the sky.
Singing his praises again and again, they all departed, resplendent in their many kinds of aerial cars.
aranya.21.cau1: When Śrī Rāma had overcome the enemy in battle, the fear of gods, men and sages alike was at an end.
Then Lakṣmaṇa returned with Sītā; he fell at the Lord's feet, and in his joy the Lord drew him to his breast.
aranya.21.cau2: Sītā gazes on his dark and tender form, and in her deep love her eyes can never have enough.
Dwelling at Pañcavaṭī, Śrī Rāma does deeds that bring joy to gods and sages.
aranya.21.cau3: Seeing Khara and Dūṣaṇa brought to ruin, Śūrpaṇakhā went and stirred up Rāvaṇa.
In a towering rage she said: You have put your realm and your treasury clean out of mind.
aranya.21.cau4: You drink and you sleep, day and night, and do not know that the enemy stands over your head.
Kingship without right policy, wealth without dharma, good deeds not offered up to Śrī Hari,
aranya.21.cau5: and learning that gives birth to no discernment: to study, to do or to gain these brings nothing but toil for its fruit.
By attachment the ascetic, by ill counsel the king, by pride knowledge, by drink modesty,
aranya.21.cau6: love that lacks humility, and by vanity the man of gifts, are swiftly brought to nothing; this is the teaching of policy I have heard.
aranya.21.so21क: An enemy, a disease, fire, sin, a master and a snake should never be reckoned small.
Saying this, she broke into lament of every kind and began to weep.
aranya.21.do21ख: She fell distraught in the midst of the court and, weeping, cried out in many ways:
O ten-headed one, while you live, should such a fate befall me?
aranya.22.cau1: At her words the courtiers started up in alarm; they soothed her, took her arm and helped her to her feet.
Rāvaṇa, lord of Laṅkā, said: Tell me your own story. Who cut off your nose and ears?
aranya.22.cau2: Śūrpaṇakhā said: The sons of Daśaratha, king of Avadh, lions among men, have come to the forest to hunt.
Their deeds have shown me that they will leave the earth without a single demon.
aranya.22.cau3: Ten-headed one, they are the ones whose strength of arm has made the sages fearless, so that they roam the forests freely.
To look at they are boys, but they are like Death itself: most steadfast, archers both, with many gifts.
aranya.22.cau4: Matchless in might and splendour are the two brothers, intent on killing the wicked and a joy to gods and sages.
The one who is a home of beauty is called Rāma, and with them is a young woman.
aranya.22.cau5: The Creator has fashioned that woman a treasure of beauty; a thousand million Ratis would be offered up for her.
His younger brother cut off my ears and nose; told that I am your sister, they mock me.
aranya.22.cau6: Hearing this, Khara and Dūṣaṇa answered my cry, but in a moment the two brothers slew the whole army.
When he heard of the slaying of Khara, Dūṣaṇa and Triśirā, Rāvaṇa burned in every limb.
aranya.22.do22: He calmed Śūrpaṇakhā and spoke of his own might in many ways.
Then he went to his palace, deep in worry, and that night sleep would not come.
aranya.23.cau1: Rāvaṇa thought: Among gods, men, asuras, nāgas and birds there is no one who can match even my followers.
Khara and Dūṣaṇa were as strong as I am; who but the Lord could have slain them?
aranya.23.cau2: If the Lord, who gladdens the gods and lifts the burden of the earth, has come down to earth in a body,
then I shall go and make him my enemy by force, and dying by the Lord's arrow, cross the ocean of worldly existence.
aranya.23.cau3: Worship will never come from this body of darkness; so in mind, deed and word this is my fixed resolve.
But if they are only princes of men, I shall seize the woman after I have beaten the two of them in battle.
aranya.23.cau4: Alone in his chariot he went off to the shore of the sea, where Mārīca had his dwelling.
Meanwhile, Umā, listen to the charming tale of how Śrī Rāma laid his plan here.
aranya.23.do23: When Lakṣmaṇa had gone into the forest to gather roots, fruit and tubers,
Śrī Rāma, all grace and joy, smiled and said to the daughter of Janaka:
aranya.24.cau1: Listen, my beloved, so fair in your vows and gentle in your ways: I am about to play a charming human part.
Until I have made an end of the demons, you must dwell within the fire.
aranya.24.cau2: The moment Śrī Rāma finished explaining it all, Sītā, holding the Lord's feet in her heart, vanished into the fire.
In her place Sītā left her own reflection, the same in nature and in form, and as modest as herself.
aranya.24.cau3: What the Lord had set in motion was a mystery hidden even from Lakṣmaṇa.
Rāvaṇa, base and bent on his own ends, went to where Mārīca was and bowed his head to him.
aranya.24.cau4: When the base bow low, great harm follows, as when a goad, a bow, a snake or a cat bends.
Pārvatī, the sweet words of the wicked are a thing to fear, like flowers that bloom out of season.
aranya.24.do24: Then Mārīca paid him honour and asked him respectfully:
Dear one, what troubles your mind so much that you have come alone?
aranya.25.cau1: The ill-fated Rāvaṇa told him the whole story with great pride, and said:
Take the shape of a false deer, full of guile, so that by this means I may carry off the king's wife.
aranya.25.cau2: Then Mārīca said: Listen, ten-headed one: he is the lord of all that moves and all that is still, in the form of a man.
Do not make him your enemy, dear one. If he slays, we die; if he grants life, we live.
aranya.25.cau3: When the prince went to protect the sage's sacrifice, Śrī Rāma struck me with an arrow that had no head,
and in a moment I was flung a hundred yojanas away. No good can come of making enemies of them.
aranya.25.cau4: I have become like the grub seized by the bhṛṅga wasp: wherever I look, I see the two brothers.
Say they are only men, dear one, still they are heroes of great valour; in opposing them you will not come through.
aranya.25.do25: He who killed Tāṛakā and Subāhu and broke Śiva's bow,
who slew Khara, Dūṣaṇa and Triśirā: can a mere man be so mighty?
aranya.26.cau1: Go back home, with the good of your family in mind. At these words Rāvaṇa burned with rage and poured out insults.
He said: Fool, do you set yourself up as my guru to instruct me? Name the warrior in all the world who is my equal.
aranya.26.cau2: Then Mārīca reasoned in his heart: To set oneself against these nine brings no good:
an armed man, one who knows one's secrets, a powerful master, a fool, a rich man, a physician, a bard, a poet and a skilled cook.
aranya.26.cau3: Seeing his death on either side, he looked to Śrī Rāma for refuge.
He thought: One word of answer and this ill-starred fellow will slay me, so let me rather fall to an arrow of Śrī Rāma.
aranya.26.cau4: With this settled in his heart he went along with Rāvaṇa; his love for Śrī Rāma's feet was never broken.
Great was the joy in his mind, that today he would see his dearest one, but he let Rāvaṇa see none of it.
aranya.26.cha1: I shall see my own most beloved Lord, and my eyes will have their reward, and I shall know joy.
On the feet of that abode of grace, with Sītā and his younger brother beside him, I shall fix my mind.
His very anger grants liberation, and devotion to him wins over even him who is subject to none;
that same Śrī Hari, ocean of bliss, will set an arrow to the string himself and strike me dead.
aranya.26.do26: Bow and arrows in hand, the Lord will run after me over the ground,
and I shall turn back again and again to look at him. No one is as blessed as I.
aranya.27.cau1: Rāvaṇa came near to that forest, and Mārīca then became the false deer.
So wondrous was it that it is past all describing; its body was made of gold, set with jewels.
aranya.27.cau2: Sītā saw the deer, lovely beyond compare, enchanting in every limb.
She said: Listen, my Lord, compassionate hero of the Raghus: the hide of this deer is very beautiful.
aranya.27.cau3: My Lord, ever true to your word, kill it and bring me its skin, says Sītā.
Śrī Rāma knew the whole cause of it; gladly he rose to bring the gods' purpose about.
aranya.27.cau4: Looking at the deer, he girded his waist, took his bow in hand and set a fine arrow to it.
The Lord gave Lakṣmaṇa careful instructions: Brother, many demons roam this forest.
aranya.27.cau5: Guard Sītā, taking thought of your wits, your discernment, your strength and the moment.
Seeing the Lord, the deer took flight, and Śrī Rāma ran after it with his bow made ready.
aranya.27.cau6: He of whom the Vedas say neti, not this, and whom Śiva cannot reach in meditation, is running after a deer of illusion.
Now it comes close, then flees far off; now it shows itself, now it hides.
aranya.27.cau7: Appearing and vanishing and playing many tricks, it drew the Lord far away in this manner.
Then Śrī Rāma took aim and loosed a deadly arrow, and it fell to the ground with a terrible cry.
aranya.27.cau8: First he called out Lakṣmaṇa's name, and afterwards in his heart he remembered Śrī Rāma.
As he gave up his life he showed his own true body, and remembered Śrī Rāma with love.
aranya.27.cau9: The all-wise Lord knew the love in his heart and bestowed on him a goal rare even for sages.
aranya.27.do27: The gods shower flowers in abundance and sing the story of the Lord's virtues.
Śrī Rāma, friend of the lowly, has given his own abode to a demon.
aranya.28.cau1: Having slain the wicked one, Śrī Rāma turned back at once, his bow shining in his hand, his quiver at his waist.
When that cry of distress reached Sītā, she spoke to Lakṣmaṇa in the utmost fear:
aranya.28.cau2: Go quickly; your brother is in grave danger. Lakṣmaṇa smiled and said: Listen, Mother.
He at the play of whose eyebrows creation dissolves — could he fall into danger even in a dream?
aranya.28.cau3: When Sītā spoke words that cut to the heart, Lakṣmaṇa's mind wavered, moved by Śrī Hari.
Entrusting her to all the gods of the forest and of the quarters, he went to where Śrī Rāma was, the Rāhu to the moon that is Rāvaṇa.
aranya.28.cau4: Finding her alone, Rāvaṇa came near in the guise of an ascetic.
He whose terror makes gods and demons afraid, so that they do not sleep at night or eat by day —
aranya.28.cau5: that same Rāvaṇa went on stealthily like a thief, glancing this way and that like a dog.
So it is, Garuḍa: when one sets foot on the wrong path, not a trace remains of bodily splendour, intellect or strength.
aranya.28.cau6: Telling pleasing tales of many kinds, he put before her statecraft, fear and love.
Sītā said: Listen, reverend ascetic: your words are those of a wicked man.
aranya.28.cau7: Then Rāvaṇa showed his own form, and when he told his name, Sītā was afraid.
Summoning all her courage, Sītā said: Stand there, wicked one; my Lord has come.
aranya.28.cau8: You have come under the sway of death, lord of the demons, like a petty hare that wants a lioness.
Hearing these words Rāvaṇa grew angry, yet in his mind he bowed to her feet and was glad.
aranya.28.do28: Then, full of rage, Rāvaṇa seated her in his chariot.
He set off along the path of the sky in haste, but he was so afraid that he could not drive the chariot.
aranya.29.cau1: Sītā cried out: Ah, Lord of the Raghus, the one hero of the world, for what fault have you forgotten your mercy?
You who take away distress and give happiness to those who seek refuge — ah, sun to the lotus of Raghu's line!
aranya.29.cau2: Ah, Lakṣmaṇa, the fault is not yours; I gave way to anger and have reaped its fruit.
Sītā lamented in many ways: the Lord, so full of grace and so loving, is far away.
aranya.29.cau3: Who will carry word of my plight to the Lord? A donkey wants to eat the sacrificial offering.
Hearing Sītā's bitter lament, all creatures, moving and unmoving, were filled with sorrow.
aranya.29.cau4: Hearing the cry of distress, Jaṭāyu, king of the vultures, knew her for the wife of Śrī Rāma, the ornament of Raghu's line.
The vile demon was carrying her off like a sacred tawny cow in the power of a barbarian.
aranya.29.cau5: Jaṭāyu said: Sītā, my daughter, have no fear; I will destroy this demon.
The bird flew at him in fury, like a thunderbolt loosed upon a mountain.
aranya.29.cau6: He cried: You there, wicked one, why do you not stand? You go on without fear; do you not know me?
Seeing him come on like Death itself, Rāvaṇa turned and reflected:
aranya.29.cau7: Is it Maināka, or Garuḍa, king of the birds? But he and his master both know my strength.
Then he knew him: This is old Jaṭāyu; he will leave his body at the holy place of my hands.
aranya.29.cau8: Hearing this, the vulture rushed at him, wild with rage, and said: Listen to my counsel, Rāvaṇa.
Let Sītā go and return home safe; otherwise, many-armed one, this is what will happen:
aranya.29.cau9: In the terrible fire of Śrī Rāma's anger your whole race will be as moths.
The warrior Rāvaṇa gave no answer; at once the vulture flew at him in anger.
aranya.29.cau10: Seizing him by the hair, he dragged Rāvaṇa from his chariot to the ground; setting Sītā aside, the vulture turned on him again.
Striking with his beak, he tore Rāvaṇa's body, and Rāvaṇa lay senseless for a daṇḍa (about twenty-four minutes).
aranya.29.cau11: Then, stung and furious, the demon drew a sword most terrible.
He cut off the bird's wings, and Jaṭāyu fell to the earth, remembering Śrī Rāma, having done a wondrous deed.
aranya.29.cau12: Seating Sītā in the chariot again, he hurried off, in no little fear.
Sītā went through the sky lamenting, like a frightened doe helpless in a hunter's grip.
aranya.29.cau13: Seeing monkeys sitting on a hill, she called the name of Śrī Hari and let a cloth fall.
In this way he carried Sītā off and kept her in the Aśoka grove.
aranya.29.do29क: The wicked one showed her fear and love in many ways and was beaten;
then he kept her beneath an Aśoka tree, having arrangements made for her keeping.
aranya.29.do29ख: The way Śrī Rāma ran off after the false deer —
that image Sītā keeps in her heart, ever repeating the name of Śrī Hari.
aranya.30.cau1: Seeing his younger brother coming, Śrī Rāma showed great anxiety outwardly.
He said: Dear brother, setting my word aside, you have come away and left Janaka's daughter on her own?
aranya.30.cau2: Bands of demons roam the forest; my heart tells me Sītā is not at the hermitage.
His younger brother clasped his lotus feet and with joined hands said: My Lord, the fault is not at all mine.
aranya.30.cau3: With his younger brother the Lord went where the hermitage was, by the Godāvarī.
Finding the hermitage without Sītā, he was as distraught as any ordinary, helpless man.
aranya.30.cau4: Śrī Rāma lamented: Ah, Jānakī, mine of virtues! Ah, Sītā, pure in beauty, character, vows and observances!
Lakṣmaṇa reasoned with him in many ways, and he went on, asking the rows of creepers and trees:
aranya.30.cau5: O birds, O deer, O lines of bees, have you seen Sītā, the doe-eyed?
Wagtail and parrot, dove, deer and fish, the hosts of bees, the skilled cuckoo,
aranya.30.cau6: jasmine buds and pomegranate, lightning, lotus, autumn moon and she-serpent,
Varuṇa's noose, Kāmadeva's bow, swan, elephant and lion are all hearing their own praise.
aranya.30.cau7: The bael fruit, gold and the plantain rejoice, without the least fear or shyness in their minds.
Listen, Jānakī: with you gone, they are all rejoicing today as if each had come into a kingdom.
aranya.30.cau8: How can you bear this rivalry? My beloved, why do you not appear at once?
So the Lord searched and lamented, as though he were a lover in deep separation, consumed by longing.
aranya.30.cau9: Śrī Rāma, whose every desire is fulfilled, the mass of joy, unborn and imperishable, was acting out a human part.
Ahead he saw the king of the vultures lying there, remembering Śrī Rāma's feet with their marks.
aranya.30.do30: Śrī Rāma, the ocean of mercy, touched his head with his lotus hand.
Gazing on the face of Śrī Rāma, the home of beauty, he was freed of all his pain.
aranya.31.cau1: Then, steadying himself, the vulture said: Listen, O Rāma, who shatters the fear of worldly existence.
My Lord, it was Rāvaṇa who brought me to this state; that wicked one has carried off Janaka's daughter.
aranya.31.cau2: My master, he has gone south with her, and she was crying out bitterly like an osprey.
I held on to life, Lord, only to see you; now, treasury of mercy, it is about to depart.
aranya.31.cau3: Śrī Rāma said: Keep your body, dear father. Smiling, the vulture answered:
He whose name, if it comes to a dying man's lips, frees even the vilest, so the Vedas sing,
aranya.31.cau4: is here before me, visible to my eyes; for want of what, Lord, should I keep this body?
With eyes full of tears Śrī Rāma said: Dear father, you have won this state by your own deeds.
aranya.31.cau5: For those in whose hearts the good of others dwells, nothing in the world is hard to win.
Leave your body, dear father, and go to my abode. What can I give you? You have nothing left to desire.
aranya.31.do31: Dear father, do not go and tell my father of Sītā's abduction.
If I am Rāma, Rāvaṇa will come there with all his family and tell it himself.
aranya.32.cau1: Leaving the vulture's body, he took on the form of Śrī Hari, with many ornaments and peerless yellow garments.
Dark of body, with four mighty arms, his eyes brimming with tears, he sang the Lord's praise:
aranya.32.cha1: Glory to you, Śrī Rāma, of peerless form, without attributes and with them, truly the mover of the guṇas.
With fierce arrows you sever the mighty arms of the ten-headed one; you are the ornament of the earth.
Your body is the colour of a rain-cloud, your face a lotus, your eyes long like lotus petals.
I bow always to the compassionate Śrī Rāma, of mighty arms, who frees us from the fear of worldly existence.
aranya.32.cha2: You are might itself, immeasurable, without beginning, unborn, unmanifest, one, beyond perception;
Govinda, beyond the senses, remover of the pairs of opposites, realised knowledge in solid form, upholder of the earth.
You delight the minds of the countless saints and devotees who chant the Rāma mantra.
I bow always to Śrī Rāma, beloved of the desireless, who crushes the host of the wicked: desire and the rest.
aranya.32.cha3: He whom the Vedas hail as stainless, Brahman, all-pervading, free of passion and unborn;
whom many sages reach through meditation, knowledge, dispassion and yoga —
he, the root of compassion, the sum of all beauty, has appeared and enchants the moving and unmoving world.
In the lotus of my heart he hovers like a bee; the loveliness of many Kāmadevas shines in his limbs.
aranya.32.cha4: He who is hard to reach and easy, pure in nature, peerless yet even to all, ever cool and calm;
whom yogis see after great effort, keeping mind and senses always in check;
that Rāma, abode of Lakṣmī, master of the three worlds, is ever at the will of his servants.
May he dwell in my heart, he who ends the round of births, whose fame makes all pure.
aranya.32.do32: Asking for the boon of unbroken devotion, the vulture went to the abode of Śrī Hari.
With his own hands Śrī Rāma performed his last rites as was fitting.
aranya.33.cau1: Śrī Rāma is very tender of heart, kind to the lowly and merciful without cause.
To a vulture, a lowly bird that fed on flesh, he gave the state that yogis pray for.
aranya.33.cau2: Listen, Umā: unfortunate are those who leave Śrī Hari and give their love to the objects of the senses.
Then the two brothers went on searching for Sītā, seeing how thick the forest grew.
aranya.33.cau3: The dense forest was crowded with creepers and trees, and there were many birds and beasts, elephants and lions.
Śrī Rāma struck down Kabandha, who came at them on the way, and Kabandha told the whole story of his curse.
aranya.33.cau4: Kabandha said: The sage Durvāsā cursed me; at the sight of the Lord's feet that sin is gone.
Śrī Rāma said: Listen, Gandharva, I tell you this: one who is hostile to the race of brāhmaṇas does not please me.
aranya.33.do33: He who sets aside deceit in thought, deed and word and serves the brāhmaṇas, the gods on earth,
has all the gods, Brahmā and Śiva and me with them, under his sway.
aranya.34.cau1: A brāhmaṇa who curses, strikes or speaks harshly is still to be revered: so the saints sing.
A brāhmaṇa should be honoured even when lacking good conduct and virtue, but not a Śūdra, however rich in virtues and skilled in knowledge.
aranya.34.cau2: The Lord explained his own dharma to him, and seeing his love for his feet was pleased at heart.
Bowing his head at Śrī Rāma's lotus feet, Kabandha regained his own state and went up into the sky.
aranya.34.cau3: Having given him that state, the generous Śrī Rāma set foot in the hermitage of Śabarī.
Śabarī saw that Śrī Rāma had come to her home; the sage's words came back to her, and her heart rejoiced.
aranya.34.cau4: Eyes like lotuses, long arms, crowns of matted hair on their heads, garlands of wild flowers on their breasts:
at the feet of the two lovely brothers, one dark and one fair, Śabarī fell and clung to them.
aranya.34.cau5: Sunk in love, she could find no words; over and over she laid her head at their lotus feet.
Then she reverently took water and washed their feet, and seated them on beautiful seats.
aranya.34.do34: She brought tubers, roots and fruits, full of sweet juice, and gave them to Śrī Rāma.
The Lord ate them with love, praising them again and again.
aranya.35.cau1: She stood in front of him with palms joined, and at the sight of the Lord her love welled up all the more.
Śabarī said: In what way am I to praise you? I am of lowly birth and very slow of mind.
aranya.35.cau2: Among those counted lowest of the low, a woman is lower still, and among them, destroyer of sin, I am dull of mind.
Śrī Rāma said: Listen to what I say, good lady: the one bond I acknowledge is that of devotion.
aranya.35.cau3: Caste, community, lineage, dharma, standing, wealth, strength, kinsfolk, virtues and cleverness: with all of these,
how does a man without devotion appear? Like a cloud that is seen to hold no water.
aranya.35.cau4: I shall tell you of devotion in its nine forms; listen with care and keep it in your mind.
The first devotion is the company of saints; the second, love for the telling of my story.
aranya.35.do35: The third devotion is service, free of pride, at the lotus feet of one's guru.
The fourth is to sing the host of my virtues, leaving all deceit behind.
aranya.36.cau1: The fifth form of worship, which the Vedas make known, is repeating my mantra and holding firm trust in me.
The sixth is self-restraint, good conduct, dispassion towards a host of activities, and being ever engaged in the dharma of the good.
aranya.36.cau2: The seventh is to see the whole world alike as full of me, and to hold the saints higher than me.
The eighth is contentment with whatever comes, and not seeing others' faults even in a dream.
aranya.36.cau3: The ninth is simplicity, guilelessness with everyone, trust in me in the heart, and neither elation nor dejection.
Whoever has even one of these nine, be it a woman, a man or any being, moving or unmoving,
aranya.36.cau4: is exceedingly dear to me, good lady; and in you devotion of every kind is firm.
Today the state that is hard to reach even for hosts of yogis has become easy for you.
aranya.36.cau5: The fruit of seeing me is supreme and beyond compare: the soul attains its own natural form.
Good lady, if you know any news of Janaka's daughter, who walks with the grace of a noble elephant, tell me.
aranya.36.cau6: Śabarī said: O Lord of the Raghus, make your way to the Pampā lake; there Sugrīva will become your friend.
He will tell you all, my Lord, O hero of the Raghus. Steady of mind, you know it all and still you ask me.
aranya.36.cau7: Laying her head at the Lord's feet time after time, she told him the whole story with love.
aranya.36.cha1: Having told the whole story, she gazed on Śrī Hari's face and set his lotus feet within her heart.
Leaving her body in the fire of yoga, she was absorbed into Śrī Hari's state, from which none returns.
O people, your many kinds of rites, your wrongdoing and your many creeds all bring grief; leave every one of them.
The servant Tulasīdāsa says: hold to faith, and love the feet of Śrī Rāma.
aranya.36.do36: He set free even such a woman, of lowly caste and a very birthplace of sins;
utterly dull mind, do you seek happiness while forgetting such a Lord?
aranya.37.cau1: Śrī Rāma left that forest too and went on; matchless in strength, the two brothers were lions among men.
Grieving like one parted from his beloved, the Lord told many stories and talked of many things.
aranya.37.cau2: Śrī Rāma said: Lakṣmaṇa, see how beautiful the forest is. Who could look at it and keep his heart unshaken?
All the flocks of birds and herds of beasts are with their mates, as though they were reproaching me.
aranya.37.cau3: When the herds of deer see us they run away, and the does say to them: You have nothing to fear.
You were born of deer; be glad. These two have come looking for a golden deer.
aranya.37.cau4: The elephants keep their mates close beside them, as if giving me a lesson.
Even a well-pondered scripture is to be looked into again and again; even a well-served king is never to be thought of as under one's control.
aranya.37.cau5: A woman may be kept within the very heart, yet a young woman, a scripture and a king are never anyone's to command.
Look, brother, at this lovely spring; without my beloved it fills me with fear.
aranya.37.do37क: Knowing me to be distraught with separation, powerless and utterly alone,
Kāmadeva, with the forest, the bees and the birds, charged down on me in one line.
aranya.37.do37ख: But his envoy saw me with my brother, and hearing his report,
the mind-born god, it seems, held back his army and then pitched camp.
aranya.38.cau1: Creepers are tangled over the great trees as though canopies of many kinds had been stretched out.
Plantains and palms are the fine flags and banners; only one whose mind is steadfast is not bewitched at the sight of them.
aranya.38.cau2: Trees of many sorts are in flower in many ways, like archers decked out in many uniforms.
Here and there handsome trees stand out, like warriors encamped apart from one another.
aranya.38.cau3: The calling cuckoos are, as it were, maddened elephants; the ḍheka and mahokha birds are camels and mules.
Peacocks, cakoras and parrots are fine horses; pigeons and swans are all Arab steeds.
aranya.38.cau4: Partridges and quails are the companies of foot soldiers; the host of Kāmadeva is beyond describing.
Mountain rocks are the chariots, waterfalls the drums, and the cātaka birds the heralds reciting his glories.
aranya.38.cau5: The humming bees are the kettledrums and pipes; the threefold breeze (cool, gentle and fragrant) has come as his envoy.
With his fourfold army about him, he roams everywhere, challenging all.
aranya.38.cau6: Lakṣmaṇa, those who stay steady at the sight of Kāmadeva's army are the ones whose name stands in the world.
His one supreme strength is woman; he who escapes her is a great warrior indeed.
aranya.38.do38क: Brother, three villains are exceedingly strong: desire, anger and greed.
Even the minds of sages who are homes of realised knowledge they unsettle in the blink of an eye.
aranya.38.do38ख: Greed draws its strength from craving and pretence; desire, from woman alone;
and anger, from harsh words: so the great sages say after reflection.
aranya.39.cau1: Umā, Śrī Rāma is beyond the guṇas, master of all that moves and does not move, and the indweller of all.
He showed how helpless are those ruled by desire, and made dispassion firm in the minds of the steadfast.
aranya.39.cau2: Anger, desire, greed, pride and māyā all fall away by Śrī Rāma's mercy.
The man on whom that conjurer looks with favour is not led astray by his magic.
aranya.39.cau3: Umā, I tell you what I have known for myself: worship of Śrī Hari is true, and all the world a dream.
Then the Lord went to the shore of a lake named Pampā, lovely and deep.
aranya.39.cau4: Its water is clear as a saint's heart, and four charming ghāṭs have been built on it.
Here and there beasts of many kinds drink its water, like a crowd of petitioners at a generous man's door.
aranya.39.do39क: Screened by the dense lotus leaves, the water is not quickly found out,
just as the attributeless Brahman, veiled by māyā, is not seen.
aranya.39.do39ख: In the fathomless water all the fish live in unbroken happiness,
as the days of the righteous pass in joy.
aranya.40.cau1: Lotuses of many colours have opened, and many bees hum sweetly.
Waterfowl and sweet-voiced swans call out, as if singing the praises of the Lord at the sight of him.
aranya.40.cau2: The flocks of cakravākas, herons and other birds must be seen; they cannot be described.
The sweet calls of the lovely birds seem to summon the travellers passing by.
aranya.40.cau3: Near the lake sages have roofed their huts, and all around are the lovely trees of the forest:
campaka, bakula, kadamba, tamāla, pāṭala, jackfruit, palāśa and mango.
aranya.40.cau4: Trees of many kinds are full of new leaves and flowers, and rows of bees sing on them.
A charming breeze blows without ceasing, cool, gentle and fragrant by nature.
aranya.40.cau5: The cuckoos call kuhū, kuhū; hearing their sweet voices, sages are drawn from their meditation.
aranya.40.do40: Bowed by the weight of their fruit, all the trees bend close to the ground,
as those who do good to others bow low when good fortune comes to them.
aranya.41.cau1: Seeing the exceedingly lovely pool, Śrī Rāma bathed in it and was supremely happy.
Finding the shade of a fine tree, Śrī Rāma sat down there with his younger brother.
aranya.41.cau2: Then all the gods and sages came there too, sang his praises and went back to their own abodes.
The compassionate Lord sat in great delight, telling his brother stories full of charm.
aranya.41.cau3: Seeing the Lord in the grief of separation, Nārada was deeply troubled at heart.
He thought: Accepting my curse, Śrī Rāma is bearing a heavy load of many sorrows.
aranya.41.cau4: I must go and see such a Lord; such a chance will not come again.
Thinking so, Nārada took up his vīṇā and made his way to where the Lord sat at his ease.
aranya.41.cau5: He was singing the story of Śrī Rāma in a gentle voice, lovingly dwelling on it in many ways.
The moment he prostrated, the Lord lifted him and kept him clasped to his heart a long while.
aranya.41.cau6: The Lord asked after his welfare and seated him close by, and Lakṣmaṇa reverently washed his feet.
aranya.41.do41: After entreating him in many ways, and knowing the Lord to be pleased at heart,
Nārada then folded his lotus hands and spoke:
aranya.42.cau1: Hear me, O Lord of the Raghus, bountiful by nature: fair boons, rare ones and easy ones alike, are yours to give.
My Lord, I have one boon to ask; grant it to me, though you know every heart and it is no secret to you.
aranya.42.cau2: Śrī Rāma said: Sage, you know my nature; do I ever hide anything from my devotee?
What thing is so dear to me, best of sages, that you could not ask for it?
aranya.42.cau3: In my mind there is nothing my devotee may not be given; never let go of this faith, even by mistake.
Then Nārada spoke joyfully: Making bold, I ask this boon:
aranya.42.cau4: Though the Lord has many names, and the Vedas say they surpass one another,
may the name Rāma, my Lord, be greater than all names, and be a hunter to the flocks of birds that are sins.
aranya.42.do42क: Let devotion to you be the full-moon night, and the name Rāma be its moon;
let the other names be the stars, and may they dwell in the clear sky of the devotees' hearts.
aranya.42.do42ख: Śrī Rāma, the ocean of mercy, said to the sage: So be it.
Then Nārada's heart filled with great joy, and he bowed his head at the Lord's feet.
aranya.43.cau1: Knowing Śrī Rāma to be very pleased, Nārada spoke again in a gentle voice:
Rāma, when you set your own māyā to work and it bewitched me — listen, O Lord of the Raghus —
aranya.43.cau2: I wished then to marry; for what reason, Lord, did you not let me?
Śrī Rāma said: Listen, sage, I tell you with emphasis: those who give up every other support and worship me,
aranya.43.cau3: I always keep watch over them, as a mother guards her child.
If a little child runs to grab fire or a snake, the mother pulls it away and keeps it safe.
aranya.43.cau4: When the son is grown, his mother still loves him, but it is not as it was before.
To me the wise man is like a grown son, and the servant without pride like an infant son.
aranya.43.cau5: My servant has my strength, while the wise man has his own; desire and anger are enemies to both.
Weighing this, the learned worship me, and even when they have gained knowledge they do not give up devotion.
aranya.43.do43: Desire, anger, greed and the rest, and pride, are the mighty army of delusion.
Among them the most dreadful and the most painful is woman, the very form of māyā.
aranya.44.cau1: Listen, sage: the Purāṇas, the Vedas and the saints say that to the forest of delusion woman is the spring.
Japa, austerity and religious observances are pools of water; woman turns into the summer and drains every one of them.
aranya.44.cau2: Desire, anger, pride and envy are frogs, and she alone is the rainy season that gladdens them.
Evil longings are a mass of night-lotuses, and to them she is the autumn, always bringing delight.
aranya.44.cau3: All forms of dharma are clusters of lotuses; becoming the frost, woman, giver of a lowly pleasure, scorches them.
Then the dense growth of javāsā that is attachment springs green again when it finds woman as its late-winter season.
aranya.44.cau4: To the flocks of owls that are sins, woman is a night of thick darkness, much to their liking.
Intellect, strength, good conduct and truth are all fish, and the skilled say that woman is like a fishing hook to them.
aranya.44.do44: The young woman is the root of faults, a giver of pain and a mine of every sorrow.
Knowing this in my heart, sage, I held you back.
aranya.45.cau1: Hearing Śrī Rāma's lovely words, the sage thrilled all over and his eyes filled with tears.
His heart cried out: Tell me, what master ever had such a way, such tenderness and love for his servant?
aranya.45.cau2: Such is the Lord, and those who will not lay delusion aside to worship him are paupers in knowledge, foolish and ill-fated.
Then the sage Nārada spoke again with reverence: Listen, Rāma, master of realised knowledge.
aranya.45.cau3: O hero of the Raghus, my Lord who breaks the fear of worldly existence, tell me the marks of saints.
Śrī Rāma said: Listen, sage, I will tell you the virtues of saints, by which I remain in their power.
aranya.45.cau4: Saints have conquered the six vices; they are sinless, free of desire, unshaken, owning nothing, pure, and homes of happiness.
Their understanding is boundless; they want nothing, enjoy in measure, hold truth as their essence, and are poets, learned men and yogis.
aranya.45.cau5: They are watchful, give honour to others, are free of pride and steadfast, and are supremely skilled in the way of dharma.
aranya.45.do45: Virtue makes its home in them; the world's sorrows do not touch them, and doubt has left them.
Apart from my lotus feet, neither their body nor their home is dear to them.
aranya.46.cau1: They shrink from hearing their own virtues and are all the more glad to hear of others'.
They are even and calm and never leave the right way; simple by nature, they have love for all.
aranya.46.cau2: They have japa, austerity, vows, restraint of the senses, self-control and observances, and love for the feet of the guru, of Govinda and of brāhmaṇas.
They have faith, forgiveness, friendliness, mercy, gladness at others' joy, and guileless love for my feet.
aranya.46.cau3: They have dispassion, discernment, humility, realised knowledge and a true understanding of the Vedas and Purāṇas.
They never practise hypocrisy, conceit or pride, and never set foot on a wrong path, even by mistake.
aranya.46.cau4: They always sing and hear of my divine play, and it is their nature to be given to the good of others without any motive.
Listen, sage: Sarasvatī and the Vedas cannot tell all the virtues that saints have.
aranya.46.cha1: Even Sarasvatī and Śeṣa cannot tell them all: the moment Nārada heard this, he took hold of the Lord's lotus feet.
So did the compassionate Lord, friend of the lowly, speak with his own mouth of his devotees' virtues.
Bowing his head again and again at the Lord's feet, Nārada went to the realm of Brahmā.
Tulasīdāsa says that those are blessed who have let go of every hope and taken on the colour of Śrī Hari.
aranya.46.do46क: People who sing and hear the purifying fame of Śrī Rāma, the foe of Rāvaṇa,
gain firm devotion to Śrī Rāma without dispassion, japa or yoga.
aranya.46.do46ख: A young woman's body is like a lamp's flame; my mind, do not be its moth.
Give up desire and pride, worship Śrī Rāma, and always keep the company of the good.
kishkindha.29.do29: When the Lord grew as he bound Bali, his body became too vast to describe.
Within two ghaṛīs (under an hour) I ran round it seven times.
kishkindha.30.cau1: Aṅgada said: I could get across, but I have some doubt in my mind about coming back.
Jāmbavān said: You are fit for everything, but you are the leader of all of us; how can we send you?
kishkindha.30.cau2: Jāmbavān, king of the bears, said: Listen, Hanumān. Why have you fallen silent, mighty one?
You are the son of the Wind and as strong as the Wind; you are a treasury of intelligence, discernment and realised knowledge.
kishkindha.30.cau3: What task in the world is so hard that you cannot do it, dear one?
You were born for Śrī Rāma's work. As soon as he heard this, Hanumān became as huge as a mountain.
kishkindha.30.cau4: His body, the colour of gold, blazed with splendour, as though he were a second king of mountains.
Roaring like a lion again and again, he said: I could leap across the salt ocean in play.
kishkindha.30.cau5: I could kill Rāvaṇa along with his helpers, then uproot Trikūṭa and bring it here.
Jāmbavān, I ask you: give me fitting counsel.
kishkindha.30.cau6: Jāmbavān said: Dear one, all you need do is go and see Sītā, then come and give us news of her.
After that the lotus-eyed Lord will do the rest by the strength of his own arms, taking the monkey army along only for sport.
kishkindha.30.cha1: With the monkey army Śrī Rāma will destroy the demons and bring Sītā back.
Gods, sages, Nārada and others will tell of his fair fame, which makes the three worlds pure.
A person who hears it, sings it, tells it and understands it reaches the supreme state.
Tulasīdāsa, a bee hovering at Śrī Rāma's lotus feet, sings it.
kishkindha.30.do30क: The fame of Śrī Rāma is the remedy for worldly existence.
Men and women who listen to it have all their wishes fulfilled by Śrī Rāma, slayer of Triśirā.
kishkindha.30.so30ख: Dark of body as a blue lotus, more beautiful than ten million Kāmadevas:
listen to the host of virtues of him whose name is a hunter to the birds of sin.
sundar.0.shloka1: I bow to him who is serene, eternal, immeasurable and sinless, the giver of the peace of liberation,
ceaselessly served by Brahmā, Śiva and Śeṣa, king of serpents, known through the Vedānta and pervading all;
who is called Rāma, the Lord of the world, teacher of the gods, Hari who through māyā (his power of illusion) appears as a man;
the mine of compassion, the best of the Raghus, the crest-jewel of kings.
sundar.0.shloka2: O Lord of the Raghus, there is no other longing in my heart.
This is the truth, and you dwell in all as their inner Self.
O best of the Raghus, grant me devotion in its fullness.
Make my mind free of desire and the other faults.
sundar.0.shloka3: I salute the son of the Wind: the home of matchless strength, his body shining like a mountain of gold,
a fire to the forest of the demons, foremost among the wise,
the treasury of every virtue, lord of the monkeys,
dear devotee of the Lord of the Raghus.
sundar.1.cau1: Jāmbavān's words were pleasing, and Hanumān was delighted at heart to hear them.
He said: Brothers, wait for me till then, bearing hardship and living on tubers, roots and fruit,
sundar.1.cau2: until I return from seeing Sītā. The work will be done; a special joy fills me.
With these words he bowed his head to everyone and, holding Śrī Rāma in his heart, set off in joy.
sundar.1.cau3: On the shore of the ocean stood a fine mountain. Hanumān leapt onto it for sport.
Remembering Śrī Rāma again and again, the mighty son of the Wind sprang up with tremendous force.
sundar.1.cau4: The mountain on which Hanumān planted his feet as he set off sank at once into the netherworld.
As Śrī Rāma's unfailing arrow flies, so Hanumān sped on.
sundar.1.cau5: The Ocean, considering that he was the messenger of Śrī Rāma, said: Maināka, be the one to relieve his weariness.
sundar.1.do1: Hanumān touched Maināka with his hand, bowed to him, and said:
Until Śrī Rāma's work is done, how can I rest?
sundar.2.cau1: The gods watched the son of the Wind on his way, and to find out how great his strength and wisdom were,
they sent Surasā, the mother of serpents. She came and spoke these words.
sundar.2.cau2: Today the gods have given me my food. On hearing her words, Hanumān said:
When I have done Śrī Rāma's work and come back and told the Lord the news of Sītā,
sundar.2.cau3: After that I will come and enter your mouth; this is the truth, mother, so let me go.
But on no account would she let him pass. Hanumān said: Then why do you not swallow me?
sundar.2.cau4: She opened her mouth a yojana wide (a yojana is some eight miles), and Hanumān made his body twice that size.
She stretched her mouth to sixteen yojanas; at once the son of the Wind grew to thirty-two.
sundar.2.cau5: However wide Surasā made her mouth, Hanumān showed a form twice as large.
When her mouth reached a hundred yojanas, the son of the Wind took on a very tiny form.
sundar.2.cau6: Going into her mouth, he came back out, then bowed his head to her and asked leave to go.
She said: The gods sent me to learn the secret of your wisdom and strength, and I have learnt it.
sundar.2.do2: You will accomplish all of Śrī Rāma's work, treasury of strength and wisdom that you are.
Blessing him, she went away, and Hanumān went on his way rejoicing.
sundar.3.cau1: A demoness lived in the ocean who caught the birds of the air by sorcery.
When creatures flew through the sky, she would see their shadows in the water
sundar.3.cau2: and seize the shadow, so that they could not fly away; in this way she always fed on those that travel the sky.
She tried the same trick on Hanumān, and he saw through her deceit at once.
sundar.3.cau3: Having killed her, the brave and steady-minded son of the Wind reached the far shore of the ocean.
Arriving there, he saw the beauty of the forest, where bees hummed, greedy for honey.
sundar.3.cau4: Trees of many kinds were lovely with fruit and flowers, and the flocks of birds and herds of animals delighted his heart.
Ahead of him he saw a huge mountain, and casting off fear he ran and climbed it.
sundar.3.cau5: Umā, in this there is no greatness of Hanumān's own; it is the glory of the Lord, which devours even Death.
Climbing the mountain, he saw Laṅkā, a fortress so extraordinary that words cannot describe it.
sundar.3.cau6: It is very lofty, with the ocean on all four sides, and its rampart of gold blazes with light.
sundar.3.cha1: Laṅkā's wall is of gold, set with gems of every colour, and within it stand many fine mansions.
With its crossroads, markets, good roads and lanes, the city is beautifully laid out in every way.
Who could count its herds of elephants, horses and mules, its foot soldiers and its many chariots?
The bands of demons who take many forms, and their army of immense strength, are beyond describing.
sundar.3.cha2: Woods, gardens, groves, flower gardens, lakes, wells and stepwells adorn it.
Maidens of men, nāgas, gods and gandharvas charm the minds of sages with their beauty.
In places, wrestlers of immense strength, with huge bodies like mountains, are roaring.
In many arenas they grapple and challenge one another in many ways.
sundar.3.cha3: Millions of warriors of fearsome build guard the city with care on all four sides.
In places the wicked demons are devouring buffaloes, humans, cows, donkeys and goats.
For this reason Tulasīdāsa has told a little of their story:
